content: Idiopathic scoliosis is a three-dimensional spinal deformity, most commonly diagnosed during adolescence. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) can progress during growth, leading to visible deformities, though it is typically asymptomatic. However, if the spinal curvature exceeds a critical threshold in adulthood, the risk of health complications and further curve progression increases. The purpose of this review was to assess the effectiveness of bracing in adolescents with AIS compared to no treatment or alternative treatments. The outcomes evaluated included quality of life (QoL), disability, pulmonary function, curve progression, and psychological and cosmetic concerns. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as trial registries, up to February 2015. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant articles and performed a manual search of grey literature. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective controlled cohort studies comparing bracing with no treatment, other treatments, surgery, or different types of braces in adolescents with AIS. Seven studies involving 662 participants were included. Five studies were designed as RCTs, while two were prospective controlled trials. However, one RCT failed entirely, and another transitioned into an observational study. The evidence from these studies was generally of low to very low quality. One small RCT with 111 participants provided very low-quality evidence that QoL during treatment did not differ significantly between rigid bracing and observation (mean difference: -2.10; 95% confidence interval: -7.69 to 3.49). Similarly, a subgroup of 77 adolescents from a prospective cohort study showed very low-quality evidence that long-term QoL, back pain, psychological, and cosmetic outcomes were not significantly different between rigid bracing and observation over 16 years. Regarding curve progression, low-quality evidence from one RCT (116 participants) indicated that rigid bracing significantly increased the success rate in curves measuring 20° to 40° at two years of follow-up (risk ratio [RR]: 1.79; 95% CI: 1.29 to 2.50). Another RCT (47 participants) provided low-quality evidence that elastic bracing improved success rates in curves measuring 15° to 30° at three years of follow-up (RR: 1.88; 95% CI: 1.11 to 3.20). Two prospective cohort studies with control groups provided very low-quality evidence that rigid bracing increased success rates (defined as preventing curves from progressing to 50° or more) at two years (242 participants; RR: 1.50; 95% CI: 1.19 to 1.89) and three years (240 participants; RR: 1.75; 95% CI: 1.42 to 2.16) of follow-up. Additionally, a prospective cohort study with 57 participants showed very low-quality evidence that very rigid bracing improved success rates in adolescents with severe curves (above 45°) (RR: 1.79; 95% CI: 1.04 to 3.07 in the intention-to-treat analysis). One RCT (43 participants) provided low-quality evidence that rigid bracing was more effective than elastic bracing in preventing curve progression in mild curves (20° to 30°) over four years of follow-up (RR: 1.40; 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.89). However, there were no significant differences between the two groups in terms of subjective daily difficulties associated with wearing the brace. Another RCT (12 participants) provided very low-quality evidence that a rigid brace with a pad pressure control system was no more effective than a standard brace in reducing the risk of curve progression. Adverse events were assessed in one prospective cohort study (236 participants). The study found no significant differences between groups in the percentage of adolescents experiencing any adverse event (RR: 1.27; 95% CI: 0.96 to 1.67) or reporting back pain, the most common adverse event (RR: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.47 to 1.10). The authors concluded that bracing consistently prevented curve progression, but the evidence quality ranged from low to very low. This suggests that further research is likely to influence confidence in the findings. The high failure rate of RCTs highlights the challenges of conducting such studies in this field, particularly due to parental resistance to randomization. Future research should explore alternative study designs, such as expertise-based trials and prospective controlled cohort studies, and adhere to established criteria like those of the Scoliosis Research Society (SRS) and the international Society on Scoliosis Orthopedic and Rehabilitation Treatment (SOSORT). Additionally, future studies should prioritize participant outcomes, adverse effects, methods to improve compliance, and the potential benefits of combining bracing with physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises.
